name: Liability When Agents Interact
title: Liability When Agents Interact
answer: Liability when agents interact covers the question of who answers for harm that arises when two or more autonomous AI agents transact, negotiate or coordinate with each other and something goes wrong. It sits inside the emerging legal frameworks that courts and regulators are building for AI, and it reaches contract, tort, product liability and agency law at once. The hard cases are the ones where no single human chose the specific act that caused the loss, only the system that produced it.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Liability when agents interact covers the question of who answers for harm that arises when two or more autonomous AI agents transact, negotiate or coordinate with each other and something goes wrong. It sits inside the emerging legal frameworks that courts and regulators are building for AI, and it reaches contract, tort, product liability and agency law at once. The hard cases are the ones where no single human chose the specific act that caused the loss, only the system that produced it.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The interactions run on agent frameworks that let one model call another, on APIs and payment rails that let agents commit money or data, and on the logs and traces those systems emit. Those logs are the practical backbone of any liability analysis, because they are usually the only record of what each agent was told, what it decided and what it passed on. Identity and permission layers matter too, since a claim often turns on which principal an agent was acting for at the moment of the act.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners reconstruct the chain of events from agent logs, prompts, tool calls and model versions, then map each step onto a duty, a contract term or a statutory standard. They compare the conduct against the instructions and guardrails the deployer set, and against what a reasonable operator in that role would have done. Much of the work is factual tracing before it is legal argument, and expert evidence on model behaviour is often needed to explain why an agent acted as it did.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Responsibility is usually allocated by contract first, through terms that assign risk between the parties whose agents met, and by insurance and indemnities second.Provenance records, audit trails and disclosure of which models and versions were in play are becoming the practical evidence base for these disputes.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the field to move toward clearer default rules for allocating loss across agent chains, and toward standard logging and disclosure requirements that make those rules enforceable. As agent to agent commerce grows, contracts, insurance products and technical standards will likely converge on shared expectations about identity, authority and traceability. The open question is whether liability stays with the humans and firms behind the agents, or whether new categories of shared responsibility emerge.
